learn.canDo: Apply the SOLID principles to a tangled class and say what each one buys and costs.
learn.why: Interviewers want to see structure that makes change cheap, and judgement about when not to add it.

learn.canDo: Match strategy, observer, factory and decorator to the problems they solve, and avoid patterns that do not fit.
learn.why: A pattern is a name for a problem. Using the right name is half of a design discussion.
learn.keyIdea: Use a pattern when you have the problem.

learn.canDo: Build an LRU cache with constant-time operations from a hash map and a linked list, and make it safe for threads.
learn.why: The LRU cache is the most common machine-coding question. The follow-up is always concurrency.
learn.keyIdea: A read that updates recency is a write.

learn.canDo: Design a parking lot with efficient allocation, extensible vehicle and pricing models, and atomic claims.
learn.why: A classic design round. The signal is allocation structure and concurrency, not the class list.
learn.keyIdea: Don't search for free spots. Keep a list of them.

learn.canDo: Model shared expenses with split strategies and integer cents, and settle a group in at most N−1 payments.
learn.why: Splitwise tests money handling and a graph reduction in one problem.

learn.canDo: Design an elevator with a state machine and a scheduler, and compare FCFS, nearest-first and LOOK on mean and worst-case wait.
learn.why: Scheduling trade-offs are the heart of this question. The tail matters more than the mean.

learn.canDo: Write a rate limiter class with a small interface, an injected clock, atomic updates and bounded memory.
learn.why: Rate limiting is asked as both a system and a class design. This is the class version.

chapter.story: The team's code works and every change is slow and risky. They practise designing classes that change cheaply.
outcomes: Reason about complexity, concurrency and memory in a class
chapter.why: Low-level design is about confining change. Every classic problem teaches a data structure choice, a concurrency question and an extension point.
chapter.payoff: In an interview you can design the usual machine-coding problems and defend the trade-offs. At work your classes will be easier to change and to test.
